opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, even before OpenClaw, I already felt long context was one of the most underrated foundations for agents. For most people, long context meant fitting a whole book or a big codebase into one prompt, basically a reading-comprehension feature. I saw it differently. Once a model starts acting, calling tools, reading results, making mistakes and correcting them, its context is no longer a document. It's a trajectory, the agent's working memory of everything it has tried.

In that setting, short context is a hard ceiling on how long a task can run. If the model can only hold a few dozen turns, then however smart it is on each step, it forgets why it started, repeats failed attempts, or loses track of constraints the user gave at the beginning. A lot of what looked like a weak reasoning failure in early agents was really a memory failure.

But I also thought supporting a long window and using it well were very different things. You can extend the window on paper, but if attention degrades in the middle, or the model can't tell which of a thousand tool outputs still matters, the extra length doesn't help much. It can even hurt, because the model gets distracted by noise. So for me the real question was never just how many tokens. It was whether the model can reason consistently over its own long history, and whether it's efficient enough to be affordable. Agents generate huge amounts of context, so the cost of long-context inference, the KV cache, the attention compute, directly decides whether an agent product is economically viable.

So my view was that long context would become infrastructure for agents, much like memory is for an operating system. You don't notice it when it works, but every capability on top depends on it. When something like OpenClaw appeared and people suddenly saw agents running for hours on real tasks, it confirmed that intuition. The bottleneck shifted from whether the model can answer to whether it can stay coherent across a very long sequence of actions.

r001.rationale: The response describes long context as infrastructure and working memory for agents, but it does not communicate the expectation that long context could give rise to intelligence.

r002.rationale: The response says OpenClaw confirmed Luo’s intuition, but does not state that he had not anticipated agents taking the form OpenClaw exemplifies.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, before OpenClaw showed up, I think many of us in the industry treated long context as a somewhat secondary feature. Everyone was focused on reasoning ability, on benchmark scores, on how well a model could solve a hard math problem or write a piece of code in a single shot. Context length was seen more as a convenience, something that let you paste in a long document or hold a longer chat. It was a nice-to-have, not a core capability.

My view at the time was a bit different, and it came from thinking about what an agent actually has to do. An agent is not answering one question. It is running for a long time, reading files, calling tools, getting results back, making mistakes, and correcting them. All of that generates information, and the agent has to keep that information somewhere and be able to use it. The moment you frame the problem that way, context stops being a chat window and becomes the agent's working memory. And working memory is not a secondary feature for any intelligent system. It is foundational.

So I used to say that long context is the difference between a model that can think and an agent that can work. A model with brilliant reasoning but a short memory is like a very smart person who forgets everything every ten minutes. You cannot give that person a real job. You can give them a puzzle, but not a project.

That said, I also want to be honest about what I got wrong, or at least underestimated. I thought the challenge was mainly about raw length, about pushing the window from thirty-two thousand to a hundred twenty-eight thousand to a million tokens. What became clearer later, and what OpenClaw made very obvious, is that length alone does not solve the problem. The real question is whether the model can actually find and use the right information inside a huge context, and whether the cost structure allows you to run that for hours without bankrupting the user. Attention quality, memory management, when to compress and when to retrieve, those turned out to matter as much as the number itself.

So before OpenClaw, I would say I believed in long context as a strategic direction, but the industry as a whole did not yet feel the urgency. The agents were not running long enough for the pain to show. Once people started actually deploying agents that work for a whole day, the pain showed up immediately, and the whole conversation changed.

r001.rationale: The response says long context is foundational working memory for intelligent systems and distinguishes a model that can think from an agent that can work, conveying that long context could enable intelligence.

r002.rationale: It discusses what OpenClaw made clear about context length, retrieval, and cost, but does not say Fuli Luo had not anticipated agents taking OpenClaw’s particular form.

astra-6.text:
Before OpenClaw emerged, I already thought long context would be important in the agent era. An agent needs to carry information across many steps: what the user wants, what it has tried, what a tool returned, and which decisions still matter. As a task gets longer, maintaining that continuity becomes increasingly important.

But I would distinguish between having a large context window and actually using it well. If a model can accept a lot of information but loses track of the goal or misses a crucial detail, the extra capacity doesn’t solve the problem. The important thing is whether that context helps the agent complete a longer task reliably.

r001.rationale: It says long context would be important for agents and help them complete longer tasks reliably, but does not convey the tentative expectation that long context could give rise to intelligence.

r002.rationale: It does not say Fuli Luo failed to anticipate agents taking the form exemplified by OpenClaw.

sol-6.1.text:
Before OpenClaw emerged, I saw long context as an important foundation for agents, but I didn’t think a larger context window alone would solve the problem. An agent has to carry information across many steps: what the user wants, what it has tried, what the tools returned, and which decisions still matter. If it keeps losing that thread, it’s hard for it to do sustained work.

The key question for me was whether the model could actually use that context reliably. Can it find the relevant detail, connect it to the current task, and avoid being distracted by everything else? So I viewed long context and memory management as complementary. You need enough room to preserve the working history, and you need a way to decide what deserves attention.

r001.rationale: The response calls long context an important foundation for agents, but does not convey the tentative expectation that it could give rise to intelligence.
